# The baselines, and what a fair comparison means {#sec-baselines}

**ISLA is measured against the two public slice-attention transformers
with the strongest record on industrial aerodynamics, GeoTransolver and
Transolver, under one protocol that fixes everything except the
architecture.** The baselines are strong, not straw: GeoTransolver has at
least as many parameters as ISLA and receives raw coordinates that ISLA
never sees; both are run at their own best learning rate; neither is ever
modified. This chapter says what each baseline computes and sees, states the
protocol as a list of rules, and settles three questions the evidence
chapters would otherwise have to carry: why every model must receive the
freestream as a unit direction, why ISLA's exact equivariance is a contract
rather than an accuracy advantage over a canonicalized baseline, and why the
learning rate belongs to the protocol.

```{python}
#| label: setup-baselines
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
J = lambda p: json.load(open(RES / p))
mean = statistics.mean
```

## The baselines and what each one sees {#sec-part-baseline}

**GeoTransolver and Transolver share ISLA's routing mechanism and differ in
what they are allowed to see: raw coordinates in a frame, and the freestream
as a raw vector.** Transolver (Wu et al., ICML 2024, arXiv
[2402.02366](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02366)) is a transformer for physics
fields on unstructured point sets. Each layer assigns every point a softmax
mixture over a fixed number of *slices*, pools point features into one token
per slice, runs attention among the slice tokens, and scatters the result
back through the same mixture: *physics attention*. GeoTransolver adds a
geometry encoder and a global-context projector. @fig-family-diagram places
ISLA beside them.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-family-diagram
%%| fig-cap: >
%%|   What each architecture is handed, and where they differ. Gray boxes
%%|   are data; the routing mechanism (solid blue) is shared by the whole
%%|   family. GeoTransolver and Transolver receive coordinates in the
%%|   dataset's frame and the freestream as a vector; ISLA receives only
%%|   invariants of the same inputs and its slices carry the surface measure
%%|   (dashed blue: fixed maps with no parameters). How to read this: the
%%|   diagram shows inputs and structure, not accuracy; the learned blocks are
%%|   the same kind of object in all three.
flowchart LR
    classDef data fill:#f4f3ee,stroke:#898781,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef learned fill:#e6f0fb,stroke:#2a78d6,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef fixed fill:#ffffff,stroke:#2a78d6,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#0b0b0b

    subgraph B["GeoTransolver / Transolver"]
        direction TB
        B1["per point: centered coordinates, unit normal<br/>global: freestream vector (unit direction under the protocol)"]:::data
        B2["GeoTransolver only: geometry encoder,<br/>global-context projector"]:::learned
        B3["physics attention × layers:<br/>softmax routing of points into slices,<br/>attention among slices, scatter back"]:::learned
        B4["linear head: pressure, wall shear"]:::learned
        B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> B4
    end
    subgraph I["ISLA"]
        direction TB
        I1["per point: position, unit normal, measure weight<br/>global: unit direction(s), scalars"]:::data
        I2["invariant seed; length unit = RMS pairwise distance"]:::fixed
        I3["slice layers × 12:<br/>measure-weighted routing, anchors,<br/>relational invariants, read-back"]:::learned
        I4["linear head on invariants → equivariant basis"]:::fixed
        I1 --> I2 --> I3 --> I4
    end
```

**GeoTransolver** is the recipe's default surface model. Per surface
point it receives the coordinates, centered on the case, and the unit normal
as a six-channel feature; the freestream vector is a three-channel global
feature. Its *geometry encoder* takes the coordinates a second time through
a dedicated embedding path that conditions the slice attention; the
ball-query local-feature path is off throughout this program, because it
is off in the recipe's shipped configuration; the GeoTransolver compared
here is therefore the one a user gets by running the recipe unmodified, not
the strongest configuration the class can express. It is not
rotation- or translation-equivariant: rotate the car and it sees a different
input (@sec-pose).

::: {#sec-transolver}
**Transolver** is the same family without the geometry encoder, the control
that isolates what the encoder contributes. Per point it receives coordinates
and normal; the freestream vector is broadcast to every point.
:::

**ISLA** receives position, unit normal and measure weight per point and the
freestream as a unit direction, consumed only through invariants and
equivariant anchors (@sec-isla). @tbl-architectures gives the three
configurations side by side.

| architecture | per-point inputs | global input | layers | hidden | slices | parameters | peak training memory at the reporting protocol (200,000 cells) |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| GeoTransolver | centered coordinates, unit normal; coordinates again through the geometry encoder | freestream vector through the global-context projector: the unit direction under the protocol | 12 | 256 | 256 | 9.0M | 80 GB |
| Transolver | centered coordinates, unit normal | freestream vector, broadcast per point: the unit direction under the protocol | 8 | 256 | 256 | 6.0M | not logged (27 GB at 100,000 cells) |
| ISLA | position, unit normal, measure weight, through invariants and anchors only | unit freestream direction | 12 | 192 | 256 | 8.9M | 27 GB |

: The three architectures compared on the aerodynamic datasets. *Per-point
inputs*: channels attached to each of the 200,000 sampled surface cells per
case under the reporting protocol. *Layers*: soft-slice attention blocks.
*Hidden*: width of the per-point feature. *Parameters*: trainable parameters
of the recipe configuration. *Peak memory*: the peak of the logged per-step
GPU memory per device over the 500-epoch protocol lane on one GB300, bfloat16
autocast, one case per step (results/isocost_reduction_2026-09-20.json;
every cost lane is in @tbl-equal-budget). How to read this: the table
states what each model is handed and what it costs, not how accurate it is.
Configuration source:
`unified_external_aero_recipe/conf/model/{isla_surface,geotransolver_surface,transolver_surface}.yaml`.
{#tbl-architectures}

### The freestream must enter as a unit direction

**The numerical scale at which GeoTransolver and Transolver receive the
freestream is a protocol variable, and on HiLiftAeroML it moves their error
more than any architectural choice in this book.** ISLA normalizes its global vector
inputs by construction. GeoTransolver and Transolver consume whatever vector
the pipeline hands them, and the dataset pipelines pass the physical
freestream velocity through without normalizing: 2,679.5 in/s on
HiLiftAeroML (the dataset is in inches and seconds) and 38.9 m/s on
DrivAerML. Coordinates and fields are nondimensionalized; this one vector is
not.

Why it matters is visible before training. GeoTransolver's global-context
projector applies linear maps and a slice softmax to the vector directly, so
its conditioning depends on the magnitude. At unit magnitude a head of the
untrained projector spreads over most of the 256 slices; at the
HiLiftAeroML magnitude it routes almost all of its weight to one
(@tbl-projector, in the note below). Transolver concatenates the raw
vector into every point's features, with the same hazard in a different
place. Training can in principle rescale either path, so these numbers are
the initialization signature; the trained measurement is what counts.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The projector's conditioning at initialization"}
```{python}
#| label: tbl-projector
#| output: asis
cond = J("geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json")["results"]
out = "| magnitude of the freestream vector | occupied slices per head (entropy-equivalent, min to max over heads) | largest context entry |\n|---:|---|---:|\n"
labels = {1.0: "1 (unit direction)", 38.9: "38.9 (DrivAerML, m/s)", 2679.5054741899685: "2,679.5 (HiLiftAeroML, in/s)"}
for r in cond:
    lab = next(v for k, v in labels.items() if abs(k - r["drive_magnitude"]) < 1e-6)
    out += f"| {lab} | {r['effective_slices_min']:.1f} to {r['effective_slices_max']:.1f} of 256 | {r['context_abs_max']:.2f} |\n"
print(out)
print(": Conditioning of GeoTransolver's global-context projector at initialization against the magnitude of the "
      "freestream vector it receives, at the recipe's projector dimensions with untrained weights. "
      "How to read this: a head that occupies one slice has lost its ability to condition on the direction; "
      "this is a property of the untrained network, and @tbl-unit-vs-physical is the trained consequence. "
      "Data: results/geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json. {#tbl-projector}")
```
:::

The trained consequence, at 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases with the same
cases, seeds and budget in both arms, is in @tbl-unit-vs-physical:
GeoTransolver and Transolver fed the unit direction are each more accurate
than their physical-velocity twin on every one of the 180 validation cases,
by a median factor above three, and both unit-direction models are ahead of
ISLA on this rung.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-unit-vs-physical
#| output: asis
fp35 = J("fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_35_2026-09-09.json")["runs"]
rf = J("relframe_reduction_2026-09-11.json")["hilift_val"]
ud = J("udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json")["paired"]
fp = lambda keys: [fp35[k]["fields"]["pressure_l2"]["fp32_mean"] for k in keys]
arms = [
    ("GeoTransolver, physical velocity, lr 1e-3", fp([f"lad_hl_gt_super_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("GeoTransolver, unit direction, lr 1e-3", fp([f"udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("GeoTransolver, unit direction, lr 3e-3 (its best at this rung)", fp([f"udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43)])),
    ("Transolver, physical velocity, lr 3e-3", fp([f"t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("Transolver, unit direction, lr 3e-3", fp([f"udrv_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("ISLA", [rf[f"rf_hl_mt2_meas_super_scarce_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]),
]
isla_ref = mean(arms[5][1])
out = "| arm | surface pressure error, seed mean (seeds) | baseline ÷ ISLA |\n|---|---|---:|\n"
for lab, v in arms:
    ratio = "—" if lab.startswith("ISLA") else f"{mean(v)/isla_ref:.2f}"
    out += f"| {lab} | {mean(v):.4f} ({' / '.join(f'{x:.4f}' for x in v)}) | {ratio} |\n"
print(out)
g, t = ud["gt_physical_35_vs_gt_unit_35"], ud["transolver_physical_35_vs_transolver_unit_35"]
print(f": The input-scale control at 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases: area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure "
      f"on the 180 shared validation cases, float32, final-epoch checkpoints, 10,000 cells, 500 epochs. Paired per case, "
      f"the unit-direction GeoTransolver is lower than its physical-velocity twin on {g['cases_where_second_is_lower']} of "
      f"{g['n_cases']} cases (median factor {g['median_ratio_first_over_second']:.1f}) and the unit-direction Transolver on "
      f"{t['cases_where_second_is_lower']} of {t['n_cases']} (median factor {t['median_ratio_first_over_second']:.1f}). "
      f"How to read this: the physical-velocity rows measure an input scale, not an architecture, and appear nowhere else in "
      f"the book as a comparison; the unit-direction rows are the protocol. Data: "
      f"results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_35_2026-09-09.json, results/relframe_reduction_2026-09-11.json, "
      f"results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json (paired counts). {{#tbl-unit-vs-physical}}")
```

Three rules follow. Every architecture receives the freestream as a unit
direction, and a comparison against a baseline fed the physical velocity is
reported only as a measurement of the input scale. The unit-direction
baseline is the reference baseline on every rung. And the input scale is
fixed by rule rather than by control: learning-rate, training-length and
seed controls vary the optimizer and cannot detect an input-scale defect.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where the hazard is small: DrivAerML and the interior task"}
At the DrivAerML magnitude the projector's concentration onto few slices at initialization is
partial (@tbl-projector), and the trained effect is nil: GeoTransolver
trained on the physical velocity and on the unit direction score within a
percent of each other at 435 cars (@sec-full-data). GeoTransolver's volume
configuration on the interior task changes by under 2% on every field
between the two inputs (@sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict), so the interior ordering
is not an input-scale effect. The rule is applied on every dataset
regardless, because a rule that depends on the dataset's units is not a
rule.
:::

## The fair-comparison protocol {#sec-fair-comparison}

**Every cross-architecture number in this book was produced under the
following rules; a comparison that violates one is not reported.** The
datasets and splits are in @sec-splits, the metric in @sec-metrics and the
training recipe in @sec-protocol.

1. **Matched cells per case: 200,000 sampled surface cells for every
   architecture, the reporting protocol.** Accuracy is flat in the cell
   count above 100,000 for every model (@tbl-cells-ladder) and is not below
   it (ISLA is 19% more accurate at 200,000 cells than at the 10,000-cell
   exploration budget on DrivAerML, and every model 20 to 25% on
   HiLiftAeroML, @sec-scoreboard-200k), so a cell mismatch
   would be a handicap disguised as an architecture difference. A number at
   any other count carries its label.
2. **Matched epochs: 500 for every arm.** Doubling GeoTransolver's budget at
   the small rungs does not lower its error (@sec-data-efficiency), and at
   435 cars and 200,000 cells 1,000 epochs move ISLA and GeoTransolver by
   0.03% each (@sec-nb-isocost-verdict), so 500 under-trains neither.
3. **Each architecture at its own best learning rate, chosen by
   validation.** ISLA runs at 1e-3 at width 192 (wider models follow the
   width rule, @sec-using-lr). GeoTransolver receives a two-rate control,
   1e-3 and 3e-3, on every rung and is reported at the better, a search
   that favors the baseline: at the reporting protocol its better rate is
   3e-3 on every DrivAerML rung and on the wings (@sec-lr-protocol).
4. **Every architecture receives the freestream as the unit direction**
   (@sec-part-baseline).
5. **Two or more seeds per cell, reported individually**, so the reader can
   see whether a ratio exceeds the seed spread.
6. **Shared validation cases**, sampled with the same seed, for every
   architecture.
7. **Paired per-case statistics where a ratio is claimed**: the count of
   validation cases on which one architecture is more accurate, with median
   and worst-decile per-case ratios, alongside the ratio of means.
8. **Sealed test splits evaluated once**, taken verbatim from the dataset
   manifest; sealed per checkpoint, not per program (@sec-splits).
9. **Preregistered bars**: each experiment states, in readout units and
   before it runs, the value that confirms and the value that refutes.

### One instrument per dataset {#sec-review-instrument}

**Every number in a family of comparisons is read from one fixed
instrument, and a control that changes the instrument is reported as a
control.** The *instrument* for a dataset is its fixed validation set and
evaluation configuration: on DrivAerML, surface pressure and wall shear on
48 held-out cars at 200,000 sampled cells, scored in float32; on
HiLiftAeroML, pressure, velocity and wall shear on 180 held-out cases shared
by every training split, at the same count and precision. An instrument is
never widened after a result is read from it; a control that changes it
(another cell count, a rotated pose, a biased sampling density) is reported
as such and never mixed into an in-family number. Its limits bind where
stated: 48 cars is a small validation set and two seeds a thin noise
estimate (@sec-limits).

## Resource matching {#sec-resource-matching}

**The parity row is matched on parameters (ISLA 8.9M against GeoTransolver
9.0M) and on cells per case (200,000, the reporting protocol), and at that
row GeoTransolver needs about 2.9x ISLA's peak training memory and 2.7x its
GPU-floor step time (80 GB against 27 GB on one GB300; @tbl-equal-budget).**
Memory was not a controlled variable in any comparison and no accuracy
result depends on it: the checkpoints in this book were trained by
implementations of the same function that differ only in footprint. Where
the two architectures are compared at unequal parameters or memory, the
section that does so says which side has more and whether it bought
accuracy.

## The comparison at equal budget {#sec-equal-budget}

**A comparison at unequal budgets is read at matched memory or matched
parameters, never down a column; cells per case are not a budget axis above
100,000.** @tbl-cells-ladder is the cell-count control behind rule 1. It
trains each architecture at its recipe width and its own best rate at
100,000 to 600,000 cells per case and scores every lane on the one
instrument, so the only variable down a column is how many surface cells a
case is sampled to. No model moves by more than its seed spread above
100,000 cells, so the capacity comparison at 100,000 cells in
@sec-shared-floor, where the frontier against memory and against
parameters is drawn, is a comparison of the architectures and not of their
cell budgets.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cells-ladder
#| output: asis
ISO = J("isocost_reduction_2026-09-20.json")["configurations"]
ladder = [("ISLA, 192 wide, 1e-3", "isla", "1e-3", (100, 200, 400, 600)),
          ("GeoTransolver, 256 wide, 3e-3", "gt_unit", "3e-3", (100, 200, 400)),
          ("Transolver, 256 wide, 3e-3", "transolver_unit", "3e-3", (100, 200, 400))]
out = "| architecture, width, learning rate | cells per case | surface pressure error (seed 42 / 43) | mean | relative to the same model at 100,000 |\n|---|--:|---|--:|--:|\n"
for lab, m, lr, cells in ladder:
    w = {"isla": 192, "gt_unit": 256, "transolver_unit": 256}[m]
    base = ISO[f"{m}|w{w}|c100k|lr{lr}|ep500"]["pressure_l2_mean"]
    for n in cells:
        c = ISO[f"{m}|w{w}|c{n}k|lr{lr}|ep500"]
        s = " / ".join(f"{v:.4f}" for v in c["pressure_l2_seeds"])
        out += f"| {lab} | {n},000 | {s} | **{c['pressure_l2_mean']:.4f}** | {c['pressure_l2_mean']/base:.3f} |\n"
print(out)
print(": The cell-count ladder on DrivAerML (435 training cars, 500 epochs): area-weighted relative L2 of surface "
      "pressure over the 48 validation cars, scored in float32 at 200,000 cells whatever the training count, two "
      "seeds. The last column divides the row's seed mean by the same model's at 100,000 training cells (below 1 is "
      "better). How to read this: a within-model control of the training cell count, not a comparison between "
      "architectures (their rows differ in width and parameters); the step from the 10,000-cell exploration budget to "
      "the protocol, which is not flat, is in @sec-scoreboard-200k. Data: results/isocost_reduction_2026-09-20.json. "
      "{#tbl-cells-ladder}")
```

## What compute should buy: cases, parameters, epochs {#sec-compute-allocation}

**Below about 100 training cases, every unit of compute belongs to more
cases; at 435 cars the data axis is near its floor and parameters buy 3 to
4% per doubling for either model; more epochs buy nothing measurable.**
That is the answer, as far as the program can give one today, to the
question a language-model practitioner would ask of a surrogate: what is
the compute-optimal mix of training set, model size and training length?
The instrument is the scaling study read together with the capacity
ladders of @sec-shared-floor: cosine-routing ISLA at three widths and
GeoTransolver at three widths, each trained for 500 epochs at 100,000
cells per case on 27, 54, 109 and 435 DrivAerML cars, two seeds, scored in
float32; the 218-car rung and the wing rungs are in @sec-program-status.
@fig-scaling-cases shows the raw picture.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scaling-cases
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Surface-pressure error against training cases for three widths of each
#|   model (cosine-routing ISLA at 192, 384 and 768 wide; GeoTransolver at 256,
#|   512 and 1,024), 500 epochs at 100,000 cells per case, two-seed means with
#|   the seeds as short bars, float32; GeoTransolver at 435 cars at the better of its two rates. Lighter shades are narrower models. The
#|   dashed reference lines have slopes of -0.7 and -0.25. How to read this:
#|   the vertical spread between shades is what parameters buy at a given
#|   training-set size (small everywhere); the slope is what cases buy, steep
#|   below 109 cars and flattening toward the shared floor near 0.040 above
#|   it. It does not show the 218-car rung or the wings. Data:
#|   results/scalelaw_interim_2026-09-21.json (27 to 109 cars),
#|   results/routenorm_cars_2026-09-21.json and
#|   results/cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json (435 cars).
#| code-fold: true
SL = J("scalelaw_interim_2026-09-21.json")["configurations"]
pts = {"isla": {}, "gt": {}}
for c in SL.values():
    if c["dataset"] == "drivaerml" and c["pressure_l2_mean"]:
        pts[c["model"]].setdefault(c["width"], []).append((c["n"], c["pressure_l2_mean"], c["pressure_l2_seeds"]))
RN = J("routenorm_cars_2026-09-21.json")["configurations"]; CAPC = J("cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json")["configurations"]
for w, key in ((192, "cars|cos|w192|lr1e-3"), (384, "cars|cos|w384|lr5e-4"), (768, "cars|cos|w768|lr2.5e-4")):
    c = RN.get(key)
    if c and c.get("mean"): pts["isla"].setdefault(w, []).append((435, c["mean"], c["seeds"]))
for w, keys in ((256, ["gt|w256|d12|s256|lr3e-3"]), (512, ["gt|w512|d12|s256|lr3e-3", "gt|w512|d12|s256|lr1e-3"]), (1024, ["gt|w1024|d12|s256|lr3e3", "gt|w1024|d12|s256|lr1e3"])):
    cands = [CAPC[k] for k in keys if k in CAPC and CAPC[k].get("pressure_l2_mean")]
    if cands:
        c = min(cands, key=lambda c: c["pressure_l2_mean"])      # each width at its better rate, as the ladders above
        pts["gt"].setdefault(w, []).append((435, c["pressure_l2_mean"], c["pressure_l2_seeds"]))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.8))
shades = {"isla": [BLUE_PALE, BLUE_LIGHT, BLUE], "gt": [RED_LIGHT, "#ec7a79", RED]}
for m, key in (("isla", "isla_ref"), ("gt", "gt")):
    kw = series_kwargs(key)
    for shade, (w, rows) in zip(shades[m], sorted(pts[m].items())):
        rows = sorted(rows); x = [r[0] for r in rows]; y = [r[1] for r in rows]
        ax.plot(x, y, marker=kw["marker"], color=shade, ls="-", lw=1.4, ms=6, label=f"{STYLE[key]['label']}, {w} wide")
        for r in rows:
            ax.plot([r[0]] * len(r[2]), r[2], ls="none", marker="_", color=shade, ms=7, mew=1.1)
for s, x0, y0 in ((-0.7, 27, 0.20), (-0.25, 109, 0.075)):
    xs = np.array([x0, x0 * 4]); ax.plot(xs, y0 * (xs / x0) ** s, color=BASELINE, ls="--", lw=1.0, zorder=0)
    ax.text(xs[1], y0 * 4 ** s, f"  slope {s}", fontsize=8, color=INK2, va="center")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xticks([27, 54, 109, 218, 435]); ax.set_xticklabels(["27", "54", "109", "218", "435"])
ax.set_yticks([0.04, 0.05, 0.07, 0.1, 0.15]); ax.set_yticklabels(["0.04", "0.05", "0.07", "0.10", "0.15"]); ax.yaxis.set_minor_formatter(mpl.ticker.NullFormatter()); ax.xaxis.set_minor_formatter(mpl.ticker.NullFormatter())
ax.set_xlabel("training cases [count]"); ax.set_ylabel("surface-pressure relative L2 error [–]")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2, loc="upper right")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scaling-exponents
#| output: asis
import numpy as np
def slope(rows, lo, hi):
    d = {r[0]: r[1] for r in rows}
    return -np.log(d[hi] / d[lo]) / np.log(hi / lo) if lo in d and hi in d else None
out = "| model | width | 27 to 54 cars | 54 to 109 | 109 to 435 | parameters, 4x: at 54 / 109 / 435 cars |\n|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|\n"
for m, name in (("isla", "ISLA (cosine)"), ("gt", "GeoTransolver")):
    ws = sorted(pts[m])
    for w in ws:
        rows = pts[m][w]; s1, s2, s3 = slope(rows, 27, 54), slope(rows, 54, 109), slope(rows, 109, 435)
        f = lambda s: f"{s:.2f}" if s is not None else "—"
        gains = []
        for n in (54, 109, 435):
            lo = {r[0]: r[1] for r in pts[m][ws[0]]}.get(n); hi = {r[0]: r[1] for r in pts[m][ws[-1]]}.get(n)
            gains.append(f"{100 * (1 - hi / lo):.0f}%" if lo and hi else "—")
        out += f"| {name} | {w} | {f(s1)} | {f(s2)} | {f(s3)} | {' / '.join(gains) if w == ws[0] else ''} |\n"
out += "\n: Local exponents of the error against training cases (the negative log-log slope between adjacent rungs, at each width) and the gain from a 15x parameter increase (narrowest to widest lane) at each rung. Data: results/scalelaw_interim_2026-09-21.json, results/routenorm_cars_2026-09-21.json, results/cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json. {#tbl-scaling-exponents}\n"
print(out)
```

**Reading the exponents.** The error is not a single power law in the
training-set size: the local exponent falls from about 0.7 between 27 and
54 cars to about 0.25 between 109 and 435 for both models
(@tbl-scaling-exponents), the signature of an approach to a floor rather
than of a scale-free law, and the floor is the one @sec-shared-floor
measures directly, near 0.040 for both architectures. Parameters are cheap
by comparison at every rung: a 15x increase buys ISLA 3 to 13% and
GeoTransolver 10 to 12%, and the capacity ladders of @sec-shared-floor
show that a further doubling at 435 cars buys 3 to 4% before turning over.
Epochs are the third axis: doubling the 500-epoch schedule to 1,000 at
200,000 cells changed neither model's error (0.0448 against 0.0448 for
ISLA, 0.0445 against 0.0445 for GeoTransolver;
results/isocost_reduction_2026-09-20.json), so the protocol is converged
and training longer is not a lever.

**The compute-optimal rule this implies.** Training compute in this recipe
is proportional to parameters times tokens seen, $C \propto P \cdot n
\cdot c \cdot E$ with $n$ cases, $c$ cells per case and $E$ epochs; cells
are flat above 100,000 (@sec-equal-budget) and epochs are converged, so
the question reduces to $P$ against $n$ at fixed $P \cdot n$. In the
Chinchilla form $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_\infty + a\,n^{-\alpha} +
b\,P^{-\beta}$ the optimum grows the axis with the *smaller* exponent once
the other's term is driven down, $P^\ast \propto C^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)}$
and $n^\ast \propto C^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}$. With $\alpha$ between 0.25
and 0.7 and $\beta$ between 0.04 and 0.06 the rule reads: *first buy cases,
each doubling of which removes 15 to 40% of the reducible error against 3
to 4% for a doubling of parameters; once the data term is small, on
DrivAerML between 109 and 435 cars, compute goes to width or depth until
the shared floor.* Three widths and four rungs do not yet separate the
floor from the parameter term, so the local exponents of
@tbl-scaling-exponents are the readout and the five coefficients are not
quoted. Two practical consequences hold now: on a dataset of a few hundred
cases the recipe's default width is the right place to spend, and a claim
that one architecture "scales better" needs the exponents, not a
single-width ladder; on the axes measured the two architectures' exponents
are the same within the resolution of two seeds.


## Pose: equivariant by construction, invariant by canonicalization {#sec-pose}

**ISLA is rotation- and translation-covariant by algebraic construction;
GeoTransolver trained in a canonical frame is exactly pose-invariant at
about a percent of accuracy cost. Against a canonicalized baseline the two
are equally good, so equivariance is a contract about what the model needs
at inference, not an accuracy advantage.** Against baselines that learn pose
from rotation augmentation instead, ISLA leads when every car arrives in a
random pose: by 12% over GeoTransolver and 21% over Transolver at the
reporting protocol, with its own error moving 1.5% between the native and
the posed evaluation (@sec-scoreboard-pose).

The two phrases mean different things. A model is *equivariant by
construction* when every operation inside it commutes with rigid motions, so
a rotated case yields the rotated prediction to roundoff (ISLA's float64
contract test, @sec-isla-contracts). A pipeline is *invariant by
canonicalization* when a preprocessing step estimates a frame from each
case, expresses the case in that frame, runs an ordinary model, and rotates
vector outputs back; it is invariant exactly when the frame estimate depends
on the pose-free geometry alone. The canonical frame used here sends the
freestream direction to +x and fixes the roll about it from the
area-weighted principal axes of the surface in the transverse plane, sign
from the third moment. @tbl-pose measures GeoTransolver on DrivAerML under
three treatments, *in pose* (cars as the dataset provides them) and on an
*SO(3) orbit* (each car in a uniformly random orientation), with vector
outputs rotated back before scoring.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pose
#| output: asis
p1 = J("p1_canonicalization_control_2026-09-02.json")
pp = J("p1pp_canonical_training_2026-09-03.json")
raw_in = [p1["table"][f"inpose|raw|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
raw_orb = [p1["table"][f"orbit|raw|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
eval_canon_in = [p1["table"][f"inpose|canon|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
eval_canon_orb = [p1["table"][f"orbit|canon|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
tr_in = [pp["results"][f"gt_canon_seed{s}"]["inpose_canon"][0] for s in (42, 43)]
tr_orb = [pp["results"][f"gt_canon_seed{s}"]["orbit_SO3_canon"][0] for s in (42, 43)]
ref = mean(raw_in)
orbit_ratios = [v / p1["prior"]["gt_inpose_pressure_l2"] for v in p1["prior"]["gt_p1_orbit_pressure_l2"].values()]
fx = lambda r: f"{r:.0f}x" if r >= 10 else f"{r:.2f}x"
def row(name, a, b):
    return f"| {name} | {a[0]:.4f} / {a[1]:.4f} ({fx(mean(a)/ref)}) | {b[0]:.4f} / {b[1]:.4f} ({fx(mean(b)/ref)}) |\n"
out = "| GeoTransolver treatment | in pose (seed 42 / 43) | SO(3) orbit (seed 42 / 43) |\n|---|---|---|\n"
out += row("trained and evaluated in the recipe frame", raw_in, raw_orb)
out += row("trained in the recipe frame, canonicalized at inference only", eval_canon_in, eval_canon_orb)
out += row("trained and evaluated in the canonical frame", tr_in, tr_orb)
print(out)
print(f": Pose dependence of GeoTransolver on DrivAerML: area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure over the 48 "
      f"validation cars, learning rate 3e-3, 500 epochs, seed 42 / seed 43, scored in bfloat16 (labeled: these runs "
      f"predate the float32 instrument and are used only for within-architecture pose factors); the parenthesized factor divides the seed "
      f"mean by the in-pose seed mean of the first row ({ref:.4f}). Across three seeds of the recipe-frame model the "
      f"orbit penalty spans {min(orbit_ratios):.0f} to {max(orbit_ratios):.0f}x. How to read this: ISLA is not shown "
      f"because its orbit and in-pose predictions agree to roundoff by construction; wall shear behaves the same way. "
      f"Data: results/p1_canonicalization_control_2026-09-02.json (rows 1 and 2), "
      f"results/p1pp_canonical_training_2026-09-03.json (row 3). {{#tbl-pose}}")
```

Three things follow (the factors are bfloat16, within-architecture, from
@tbl-pose). GeoTransolver in the recipe frame is not pose-robust: a random
orientation multiplies its error by more than twenty. Canonicalization must
be in the training pipeline: applied only at inference to a model trained in
one exact pose it is pose-invariant but costs 1.6 to 1.7x, because that model is hypersensitive to the sub-degree tilt of the frame
estimate, and a model that sees the estimator's tilt noise during training
learns to ignore it (third row). And on this data ISLA's exact equivariance
and canonicalized GeoTransolver deliver the same pose invariance, so no
accuracy claim in this book is attributed to equivariance; the pose contract
is scored as a contract.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What the contract still buys"}
Canonicalization needs a known global direction at inference and a
principal frame whose sign can be resolved; both hold for every vehicle and
wing here (no DrivAerML case is within 5% of a principal-axis degeneracy).
They fail for a PDE surrogate with no distinguished global direction, for
bodies whose transverse inertia tensor is degenerate or whose third moment
vanishes, and for assemblies of parts in mixed orientations, where no single
frame canonicalizes every component. ISLA needs neither a frame estimate nor
a global direction at inference; there the contract is the difference
between a working surrogate and the first row of @tbl-pose. Against
baselines that learn pose from augmentation rather than from a canonical
frame, the contract also earns accuracy (@sec-scoreboard-pose).
:::

## Learning-rate sensitivity is part of the protocol {#sec-lr-protocol}

**The architectures lose very different amounts of accuracy at a wrong
learning rate, so a protocol sharing one rate would measure tuning luck
instead of architecture.** One grid step above its best rate,
GeoTransolver's seed-mean error grows 9.0x on DrivAerML and 6.5x on
HiLiftAeroML (full splits, 10,000 cells, bfloat16, within-architecture;
results/instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json,
results/highlift_wave_reduction.json). ISLA fails differently above its
rate: at 3e-3 it reaches the mean-field plateau defined in @sec-using-lr,
total routing collapse. Under linear routing the rate that avoids the
plateau falls like 1/width and at least 1/depth, which is the width
learning-rate rule of @sec-using-lr; the cosine form of the routing softmax
(@sec-isla-slices) bounds the routing logits and removes the ceiling on
every DrivAerML lane tested (@sec-nb-routenorm-cars-verdict). At width 192
ISLA runs at 1e-3 throughout, and the point here is procedural: each
architecture runs at its own best rate. GeoTransolver's best rate also
depends on how much data it sees: at the reporting protocol of 200,000
cells, 3e-3 beats its 1e-3 lanes by 31%, 24%, 10%, 4% and 2% at 27, 54,
109, 218 and 435 DrivAerML cars; every 200,000-cell row therefore uses
GeoTransolver at 3e-3 and names it (@sec-scoreboard-200k,
@sec-nb-rategt-prereg).

Two consequences are built into the protocol. Because GeoTransolver's best
rate differs between datasets and between budgets, "best rate per
architecture" is the only rule under which the baseline is the strongest
version of itself; at the reporting protocol the rate choice moves the
27-car row by 31% and decides it (@sec-scoreboard-200k). GeoTransolver
received a two-rate control on every DrivAerML rung at the reporting
protocol and the better rate is reported, a search ISLA cannot use because
it has one usable rate (@sec-robustness-lr). Rate, training-length and seed controls at the small splits move
GeoTransolver's error by far less than its input-scale sensitivity
(@tbl-unit-vs-physical), which is why the input scale is fixed by rule and
not tested by control.
